chapter: New York dance bands and Dorsey
title: Claude Thornhill's exit from the Rainbow Room
summary: Thornhill leaves the Noble band by announcing his departure from the stage with an armload of music cases.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: Once he stopped he was able to go out and become a big success. But there are so many funny stories of course to tell about the experience with Ray Noble, as I say he was a great musician and he wrote some beautiful songs, but he and Claude Thornhill didn't get on too well and I will never forget the night Claude left. Now In the Rainbow Room you had a big stage like in the back, on either side of the platform stage were two flights of stairs and the acts would or were run up under a spotlight, They would come out of a velvet curtain and down the stairs, running down and on to the dancefloor to do their acts.

Some of the best acts in the world and it was so funny to hear Ray Noble introducing these acts, 'Now, ladies and gentlemen, from the continental (unintelligible) we have so and so, and the people didn't have the faintest idea what he was saying. It was all a lot of fun.

And the night that Claude Thornhill decided to leave, he got up -- now, in those days, we had these sort of plastic-paper combination like music cases and they were very fancy, with our names on them, Ray and his orchestra, very expensive, and they were paperweight without

of course, music in them and Claude got all of those and Claude had this sort of straw-like, sandy-like hair, and he combed it all down to the sides and was monstrous looking and he was the funniest little man in the world, anyway, being the fine musician he was, he was crazy. He got up on the stage and the spotlight is on him because somebody in the house thought it was an act, and he's going to leave and he has all these music cases, all over, like a -- like stocks of bananas, you know, and he's looking down at the people, all laughing like hell, and he said, 'Ladies and gentlemen, I'm going to leave and this is the last time you'll ever see me. Goodbye.' And he left and we never saw him again.
And an hour later, Ray Noble looked at his watch and he said, For God's sake, where's Claude? Well, anyway, that was it.
The next time I was to hear of Claude, he had a big band. Writing serious music.
Ray didn't realize what was going on.
Ray didn't have the faintest idea that Claude was leaving. But that was Claude's crazy way of leaving the band, instead of going through the two weeks' notice -- pardon.
And then he had that good band.
